tools.hubLead: Free mahjong tools that read your tiles for you — check what a hand is waiting for, work out what it scores, and look up any tile by sight.
tools.hubIntro: Pick a tool below. Everything runs in your browser, nothing is uploaded, and no download is needed.
tools.inDevelopmentNote: Coming soon — this calculator is still being built.
tools.readingNote: New to mahjong? These guides explain the ideas behind the numbers.
tools.waitsLead: Tap the tiles in your hand and find out what it is waiting for — how far it is from ready, and which tiles would complete it.
tools.waitsMetaDesc: Free mahjong hand checker. Enter your hand to see its shanten, every winning tile, and how many of each are still unseen. Runs in your browser, no download.
tools.waitsPickHint: Tap a tile to add it. Tap a tile in your hand to remove it.
tools.waitsIncomplete: Add {n} more tiles to check this hand.
tools.waitsIncompleteHint: A hand can be checked at 13 tiles, or 10, 7 and 4 when part of it is exposed.
tools.waitsWinningHint: The tiles you entered already form a complete hand.
tools.waitsAwayHint: You need to swap {n} tiles to reach a ready hand.
tools.waitsRemainingNote: Counts are based on your hand only — tiles already discarded are not included.
tools.waitsImproveNote: Each of these brings you one step closer to ready.
tools.waitsShantenWhat: Shanten counts how many tile swaps you still need before the hand is ready to win. 0 means the hand is ready; -1 means it is already complete.
tools.waitsHowTitle: How to use the hand checker
tools.waitsHowP1: A mahjong hand checker is for the moment when you are staring at thirteen tiles and cannot tell whether the shape is close. Tap every tile you are holding into the grid above. There is no submit button: the mahjong hand checker updates as soon as the count is one that can be read — usually thirteen for a fully concealed hand, or ten, seven or four when part of the hand is already exposed on the table.
tools.waitsHowP2: What you get back is three answers at once. First, shanten: how many tile swaps still stand between this hand and a ready shape. Second, if the hand is already ready, the exact waiting tiles that would complete it. Third, when the hand is not ready yet, the useful tiles that would bring the shape one step closer. Those three readings are the same ideas players argue about at the table — distance, waits, and acceptance — spelled out without requiring you to do the combinatorics yourself.
tools.waitsHowP3: The remaining-count figure next to each waiting or improving tile only subtracts copies that appear in the hand you entered. It does not know what other players discarded or melded, because the checker cannot see the table. Treat that number as an upper bound: on a live table some of those copies may already be gone. That honesty is deliberate — a precise wall count would be a lie when the tool only sees your tiles.
tools.waitsHowP4: Shareable links are part of the design. As you tap tiles, the address bar quietly stores the hand in a `hand` query string. Copy the URL, paste it into a chat or forum post, and anyone who opens it sees the same hand and the same reading. Illegal or truncated codes are ignored rather than throwing an error, so a broken paste never bricks the page.
tools.waitsHowP5: This mahjong hand checker follows Hong Kong mahjong for the shapes it recognises — runs, triplets, pairs, seven pairs and thirteen orphans. Those building blocks overlap with most regional variants, so the distance reading is a useful guide even if your home table scores differently. Scoring itself is a separate question; when you already know what you are waiting for, the score calculator answers how many fan the completed hand is worth.
tools.waitsHowP6: Use the checker while you play elsewhere: keep it in a second tab, mirror your current hand, and read the answer before you discard. Because the numbers come from the same engine that powers the practice tables on this site, a hand that looks ready here will look ready in a Hong Kong game here too. That consistency is the whole point of a checker that claims to read tiles rather than guess.
tools.waitsFaqA1: Shanten is the number of tile swaps you still need before the hand is ready to win. A hand with a shanten of 2 needs two useful tiles before it can win; a shanten of 0 means it is ready and any winning tile completes it.
tools.waitsFaqQ2: Why does my hand not show a result?
tools.waitsFaqA2: A hand can only be read at certain sizes. Enter 13 tiles for a concealed hand, or 10, 7 or 4 when part of the hand is already exposed. Any other number of tiles cannot form a legal hand, so the checker waits.
tools.waitsFaqQ3: Does this use the tiles that have been discarded?
tools.waitsFaqA3: No. The checker only sees the tiles you enter, so the remaining counts are based on your hand alone. On a real table some of those tiles will already be gone.
tools.waitsFaqQ4: Which mahjong rules does this follow?
tools.waitsFaqA4: This version follows Hong Kong mahjong. The shapes it looks for — runs, triplets, pairs, seven pairs and thirteen orphans — are shared with most mahjong variants, so the result is a useful guide for almost any table.
tools.waitsFaqA5: No. The checker runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you enter leaves your device and nothing is stored.
tools.tileIdLead: Not sure what a tile is called? Tap it to see its name, its suit, and the other names players use around the world.
tools.tileIdMetaDesc: Identify any mahjong tile. Tap a tile to see its name, suit, rank and the alternative names — Bams, Craks, Dots, Soap and more. Free, no download.
tools.tileIdPickHint: Tap any of the 34 tiles. The detail panel updates immediately — no submit button.
tools.tileIdTipChow: With neighbours of the same suit it can form a chow (run of three).
tools.tileIdTipPong: Three identical copies make a pung (triplet).
tools.tileIdTipKong: Four identical copies make a kong.
tools.tileIdTipFlush: A full flush uses tiles from only one numbered suit.
tools.tileIdCatalogLead: Every playable tile is listed below with its English name and the nicknames players use. Each tile has a shareable anchor — for example #s3 for the 3 of Bamboo.
tools.tileIdHowTitle: How to use the tile identifier
tools.tileIdHowP1: A mahjong tile identifier answers a question beginners ask constantly: what is this tile called? Tap any face in the grid. The panel shows the standard English name, the suit, the rank when it is a number tile, and the other names you will hear at different tables — Craks and Man for characters, Circles and Pins for dots, Bams and Sou for bamboo, Soap and Po for the white dragon.
tools.tileIdHowP2: The full catalogue further down the page is not decoration. Every one of the 34 tiles is rendered in the HTML so search engines and shared links can land on a specific tile. Open /tools/tile-identifier#s3 and you jump straight to Three of Bamboo. That makes the page a durable reference, not only an interactive widget.
tools.tileIdHowP3: Names differ by language and by region. American players say Bams and Craks; Japanese tables say Sou and Man; Cantonese tables use 条子 and 万子. The identifier lists those aliases side by side so a nickname you heard online still maps back to the same physical tile. The white dragon lists Soap and Po because those are real American calls — it never renames the tile as a colour dragon.
tools.tileIdHowP4: Once you can name the tiles, the next questions are usually about shape and score. The hand checker tells you how far a set of tiles is from ready. The score calculator (when available) reads a completed Hong Kong hand and lists every pattern it matches. This identifier stays focused on recognition so it stays fast to open while you learn.
tools.tileIdHowP5: Use it beside a physical set, a screenshot, or another site. Nothing you tap is uploaded. The page is free, needs no download, and keeps the same 34-tile set the Hong Kong practice tables on this site use — no flowers, no red fives, just the tiles you actually draw in the games here.
tools.tileIdFaqQ1: How many tiles does the identifier cover?
tools.tileIdFaqA1: All 34 kinds used in Hong Kong mahjong: nine characters, nine dots, nine bamboo, four winds and three dragons. Flowers, seasons and red fives are omitted because they are not part of the Hong Kong set this site plays.
tools.tileIdFaqQ2: Why does the white dragon list Soap?
tools.tileIdFaqA2: Soap and Po are common American nicknames for the white dragon tile. They are listed as aliases so players who learned those names can still find the tile. The Chinese name remains 白板 — the site never calls it a white dragon in Chinese copy.
tools.tileIdFaqQ3: Can I link to a specific tile?
tools.tileIdFaqA3: Yes. Each tile has an anchor equal to its id, such as #m1 or #z5. Share that URL and the page opens scrolled to that tile in the catalogue.
tools.tileIdFaqQ4: Are the pictures the same as in the games?
tools.tileIdFaqA4: Yes. The identifier uses the same tile faces as the practice tables, so the tile you learn here looks like the tile you will see when you play.
tools.tileIdFaqA5: No. Recognition only. For shanten and waiting tiles use the hand checker; for Hong Kong fan values use the score calculator.

tools.scoreHowTitle: How to use the score calculator
tools.scoreHowP1: Most mahjong calculators ask you to count fan and fu yourself, then convert that number into points. This mahjong score calculator reads the tiles. Enter a completed Hong Kong hand, mark the winning tile, choose self-draw or discard, and the tool matches the hand against the patterns the site engine already uses at the table.
tools.scoreHowP2: Hong Kong scoring is fan-based. Standard tables need three fan to declare a win; casual chicken-hand tables are a different mode and are not the default here. Patterns such as all simples, a dragon pung, or a self-draw each contribute fan, and limit hands such as big three dragons or thirteen orphans sit at the top of the scale.
tools.scoreHowP3: The calculator rebuilds a minimal game state with createGame, then calls the same scoreHand function the practice tables use. Defaults are East seat and East round so seat-wind and round-wind fan are included when your hand has those pungs. Open advanced options to change either wind before scoring.
tools.scoreHowP4: If the tiles do not form a winning shape, you get a clear message and a link to the hand checker instead of a fake total. If the hand wins on paper but has fewer than three fan, the patterns are listed with an explanation that the minimum has not been met — the tool never pretends a 1-fan hand is a legal win on a standard table.
tools.scoreHowP5: Japanese riichi calculators will not answer Hong Kong questions correctly: pinfu is worth zero fan here, and several riichi-only yaku do not exist. Use this page for Hong Kong mahjong, and keep riichi tools for riichi tables. Everything runs in your browser with no upload and no download.
tools.scoreFaqQ1: Does this calculator count patterns or only convert fan?
tools.scoreFaqA1: It reads the hand and matches patterns. You do not enter a fan total yourself — that is the difference from most online converters.
tools.scoreFaqA2: Hong Kong mahjong in standard mode (3-fan minimum). Casual chicken-hand scoring is not the default on this page.
tools.scoreFaqQ3: Why are seat wind and round wind defaults East?
tools.scoreFaqA3: A rebuilt practice state needs winds to score wind pungs. East/East is the createGame default and is stated in the UI. Change them under advanced options when your seat or the round differs.
tools.scoreFaqQ4: What if my hand is not complete?
tools.scoreFaqA4: The score calculator only scores winning hands. Use the mahjong hand checker to measure shanten and waiting tiles first.
tools.scoreFaqA5: No. Scoring runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is stored or sent to a server.
tools.hubAboutP2: Every tool here reads your tiles directly rather than asking you to count by hand. Most scoring calculators online are converters: they assume you already worked out the fan and the fu yourself, and they only turn that number into points. These tools start from the hand, match it against the patterns, and show you the reasoning.
tools.hubAboutP3: This set follows Hong Kong mahjong, the variant most often played in Cantonese-speaking regions and the one this site is built around. If you have been searching for a mahjong calculator and finding only Japanese riichi tools, this is the gap they leave.

tools.waitsConceptsP1: A mahjong hand is not a pile of tiles, it is a set of blocks: four groups of three plus a pair. Shanten measures how far the hand is from that shape, counting the swaps still needed. A hand at shanten 4 is a long way out; a hand at shanten 1 needs a single useful tile. The number is not a prediction of who wins, it is a reading of how close the shape is.
tools.waitsConceptsP2: When shanten reaches 0 the hand is tenpai — ready. That is the point where the question changes from "what do I keep" to "what am I waiting for". A wait can be wide or narrow: a hand waiting on three kinds of tile can be completed by twelve tiles, while a single-tile wait may be down to two or three live copies. Two tenpai hands can look equally ready and be worth very different amounts, which is why a checker shows the waiting tiles rather than only the shanten.
tools.waitsOverfull: That is 14 tiles — take one back out and the checker will read the hand.
tools.hubFaqA1: Yes. Every calculator on this page is free to use, with no account and no download. The tools run entirely in your browser, so nothing you type is uploaded and nothing is stored.
tools.hubFaqQ2: Which mahjong rules do the calculators follow?
tools.hubFaqA2: Hong Kong mahjong. This is the variant played across Cantonese-speaking regions, and it is the ruleset this site is built around. Japanese riichi uses different tile patterns and different scoring, so a hand that scores here may score differently in a riichi calculator.
tools.hubFaqQ3: Do I need to know how to count fan or fu myself?
tools.hubFaqA3: No, and that is the point. Most mahjong calculators online are converters: they ask you to count the fan and fu yourself, then convert that total into points. These tools read the hand directly, work out which patterns it matches, and show the reasoning.
tools.hubFaqQ4: Can I use these tools while playing on another site?
tools.hubFaqA4: Yes. Open a tool in a second tab, enter the tiles you are holding, and read the answer. The hand checker runs the same engine as the games on this site, so the reading you get in a game and the reading you get in the tool will not disagree.

catalog.hallLead: Free online mahjong on this site covers three moods: four-player tables against AI, Mahjong Solitaire match-and-clear boards, and Mahjong Connect path puzzles. Pick a category below, or open a featured game and start in your browser — no download and no account required.
catalog.hallAboutTitle: How to choose a mahjong game
catalog.hallAboutP1: If you want a short break with familiar tile art, start with a puzzle. Mahjong Solitaire clears a stacked layout; Mahjong Connect joins matching tiles on a flat grid. Both are single-player and you can pause whenever you like.
catalog.hallAboutP2: If you want the classic four-player game, open Play vs AI. Hong Kong, Riichi, Chinese Official, Sichuan, Taiwanese and American practice tables sit side by side so you can try the ruleset you keep hearing about without waiting for three friends.
catalog.hallAboutP3: New to the tiles? Read a short guide first, then come back and pick a board. Everything on this hall page is free entertainment — there is no real-money betting and no purchasable gambling currency.
catalog.hallFaqQ1: Do I need to download an app?
catalog.hallFaqA1: No. Every game here runs in the browser. Open a page, wait for the board, and play.
catalog.hallFaqQ2: Which game should a complete beginner open first?
catalog.hallFaqA2: Mahjong Solitaire is usually the gentlest start: one player, clear goals, and no scoring jargon. When you want the real table game, open a Hong Kong practice table against AI.
catalog.hallFaqQ3: Is Mahjong Solitaire the same as four-player mahjong?
catalog.hallFaqA3: No. Solitaire is a single-player matching puzzle. Four-player mahjong is a turn-based table game with melds, discards and scoring. They share tile art, not rules.
catalog.hallFaqA4: Yes. You can play without signing in. An account only saves points and progress if you want them.
catalog.classicLead: Play real four-player mahjong against AI at your own pace. This category gathers Chinese, Japanese, American, Taiwanese and Sichuan practice tables so you can learn a ruleset without waiting for a full room. Each card opens a dedicated board with its own scoring and callouts.
catalog.classicAboutP1: Hong Kong mahjong is a fan-based Cantonese table — a clear place to learn melds, discards and self-draw versus discard wins. Japanese Riichi adds ready declarations, dora and a different payment style. Chinese Official (MCR) uses a large point chart and an eight-point gate before a hand may win.
catalog.classicAboutP2: Sichuan blood-battle tables focus on a missing suit and consecutive winners. Taiwanese sixteen-tile play uses a longer hand and tai-based settlement on this site’s baseline. American practice covers Charleston exchanges and jokers without copying trademarked NMJL card patterns.
catalog.classicAboutP3: All of these seats are AI partners. You never wait for three humans, and you can switch rulesets whenever you want a different scoring language. Open a card below when you are ready to sit down.
catalog.classicFaqQ1: Do I need three other people?
catalog.classicFaqA1: No. Three seats are AI. You can start a hand alone and play at your own speed.
catalog.classicFaqQ2: Which ruleset should I try first?
catalog.classicFaqA2: Hong Kong is a friendly first table if you are new to four-player play. Switch to Riichi or Chinese Official once you want a different scoring language.
catalog.classicFaqA3: No. These are free practice tables. There is no buy-in, no cash-out, and no purchasable gambling currency.
catalog.classicFaqQ4: How is American mahjong handled here?
catalog.classicFaqA4: This site offers an American-style practice table with Charleston and jokers. It does not reproduce trademarked NMJL card patterns.
catalog.solitaireLead: Mahjong Solitaire is the single-player tile puzzle most people mean when they search for mahjong online. You clear a stacked layout by matching identical free tiles until the board is empty. It is not the four-player table game — there is no turn order, no scoring patterns to declare, and no opponents. Overseas players who type “mahjong” into a search box are often looking for this relaxing match-and-clear experience first.
catalog.solitaireAboutTitle: What Mahjong Solitaire is — and what it is not
catalog.solitaireAboutP1: Mahjong Solitaire and Mahjong Connect use the same tiles but are different puzzles. Solitaire stacks tiles in layers: you only take a tile that is free on top with an open side. Connect lays every tile flat on a grid and asks you to join two identical faces with a path of at most two turns. If you want a layered clear-the-mountain feel, stay with Solitaire. If you prefer a flat maze, open Mahjong Connect instead.
catalog.solitaireAboutP2: Layouts differ mainly by shape and height. Turtle builds a tall, symmetric mountain that feels dense in the middle. Pyramid rises in stepped tiers and usually plays a little more open. Both are the same matching game — the difference is how crowded the free edges feel as you dig down.
catalog.solitaireAboutP3: Traditional four-player mahjong is a turn-based table game of melds, discards and scoring. Solitaire is a solitary puzzle that only shares the artwork. When you want a fixed classic layout such as turtle or pyramid, open Mahjong Solitaire Classic for the playable board.
catalog.solitaireFaqQ1: Should I play Solitaire or Connect?
catalog.solitaireFaqA1: Choose Solitaire for stacked layouts and matching free tiles. Choose Connect when you want a flat grid and path-finding between identical tiles. They are siblings, not the same game.
catalog.solitaireFaqQ2: Which is better for absolute beginners?
catalog.solitaireFaqA2: Solitaire is usually gentler: the goal is simply to clear the board. Connect adds path limits that can feel trickier on the first try.
catalog.solitaireFaqQ3: How does this relate to four-player mahjong?
catalog.solitaireFaqA3: Only the tiles look familiar. Four-player mahjong is a multiplayer table game with scoring. Solitaire is a one-player puzzle with no discards and no fan counting.
catalog.solitaireFaqQ4: Do I need to download or register?
catalog.solitaireFaqA4: No. Open the classic board in your browser and play free. An account is optional and only saves progress if you want it.
catalog.solitairePlayClassic: Want a fixed classic layout (turtle / pyramid)? Open Mahjong Solitaire Classic.
